title: "Final Project"

The final project integrates conceptual understanding with applied statistical skills in R. You will identify a research question, analyze a real criminal justice dataset, and interpret your findings using the tools from this course — building it **incrementally across the second half of the semester** rather than in a December scramble.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**Due: via Canvas by 11:59 pm the Sunday before Session 13.** You then present in class at Session 13. There will be *absolutely* no assignments or projects accepted after the Sunday deadline. None. Add it to your calendar now. Failure to submit any part by the deadline results in a zero. No appeals. Plan ahead.
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Want to see what "done well" looks like?** A complete worked example — report structure, code, both-traditions model, honest limitations — is at the [project exemplar](final-project-exemplar.qmd).
:::

## The timeline (how the project is paced)

| When | Milestone |
|------|-----------|
| Session 6 | Start scouting datasets (guidance in class) |
| **Session 7** | **Dataset selection due** (workshop day — you'll work with your data in class) |
| Session 8 HW | Checkpoint 1: descriptives + a plot of your outcome variable |
| Session 10 HW | Checkpoint 2: measures of association among your key variables |
| Session 11 HW | Checkpoint 3: a first regression model |

By presentation day, every piece of your analysis will already exist — the project is assembled, not started, at the end.

## 1. Purpose

Demonstrate your ability to apply statistical reasoning and R coding skills to a real-world criminal justice dataset: identify a research question, analyze data, and interpret findings using the concepts learned throughout the course.

## 2. Project components

Your submission must include **all** of the following:

- **R script (`.R`)** — fully runnable code that produces your results
- **Your dataset** — submitted so I can reproduce your analysis
- **Output** — tables, figures, and statistical output from R, as applicable, incorporated in your written report
- **Written report (`.docx`)** — a short report (3–5 pages) explaining your research question, dataset, methods, results, and interpretation

## 3. Steps and expectations

**Step 1 — Find a dataset.** Select a dataset related to criminal justice (policing, courts, corrections, crime, public opinion, etc.) that can be imported into R (CSV, Excel, or an R dataset). It must include enough numeric variables for regression analysis. *(Formal selection criteria and the submission form are part of the [Session 7 assignment](homework/hw-07.qmd).)*

**Step 2 — Define your research question.** Keep it focused and testable. Examples: *"Are violent crime rates associated with police staffing levels?"* or *"Do education and income predict victimization (or arrests)?"*

**Step 3 — Apply statistical tools from class.** Use descriptive statistics, visualizations, and measures of association. You **must** include a linear regression or logistic regression for credit. **Your final model must be reported in both traditions** — the frequentist fit (`lm()`/`glm()`) *and* the Bayesian fit (`brm()`, default priors are fine — say so) — with at least one sentence comparing what each tells you (e.g., the CI vs. the credible interval, or what the posterior lets you say that the p-value doesn't). This is the both-traditions course; the capstone shows you can drive both. Supporting analyses (descriptives, correlations) may be run in whichever tradition you prefer.

**Step 4 — Write and submit your report.** Organize clearly: Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion. Interpret results in plain language.

## 4. Grading criteria

The project is **30% of your course grade**: the written report, script, and output are **22%**, and the in-class presentation is **8%**.

### The written report & code (22% of course grade)

| Criterion | Weight | Excellent | Adequate | Needs work |
|---|:---:|---|---|---|
| **Quality of analysis** | 7% | Right tools for the question; final model in **both traditions** with sound model choices; assumptions/diagnostics addressed | Correct core analysis; both traditions present but one is perfunctory; minor tool misfits | Wrong tool for the question, a missing tradition, or mechanical errors that change conclusions |
| **Interpretation & honesty** | 6% | Every claim matches the output; magnitude interpreted in real units; limitations (incl. null or weak results) owned plainly | Mostly accurate; occasional overclaiming or a p-value/posterior misreading; limitations thin | "Significant" treated as "important"; causal language from observational data; results oversold |
| **Organization & writing** | 4% | Clear Introduction → Methods → Results → Discussion; labeled figures/tables referenced in text; graduate-level prose | Structure present but uneven; figures unlabeled or orphaned | Hard to follow; output pasted without narrative |
| **Completeness & reproducibility** | 5% | Script runs top to bottom on the submitted data; all four components present; seed set where results are sampled | Runs with minor fixes; a component thin but present | Script errors out, data missing, or a required component absent |

### The presentation (8% of course grade)

**Format: 8 minutes + 2 minutes of questions.** Presentation order is announced at the Session 12 code clinic. You may present slides or your rendered report on screen — either is fine, but you **must show your one key visualization** and be ready to walk through **any line of your code** on request (see the [AI policy](syllabus.qmd#use-of-artificial-intelligence-tools); not being able to explain your own code will cost you well beyond the presentation points).

| Criterion | Weight | What earns it |
|---|:---:|---|
| **The question, motivated** | 2% | A listener knows within a minute what you asked, of what data, and why anyone should care |
| **Sound interpretation, limits included** | 3% | Findings stated accurately with magnitudes; at least one limitation named without prompting; questions handled honestly (including "I don't know") |
| **The key visualization** | 1.5% | One figure that carries the finding, readable from the back of the room, honestly captioned |
| **Code ownership** | 1.5% | Any line of your script, explained on request, in your own words |

Running long is the classic failure: **practice once with a timer**. At 8 minutes you'll be stopped so everyone presents.

Submit all files via **Canvas before midnight the Sunday before Session 13**. Late submissions will not be accepted. You will present your project during class at Session 13.
